report.source_text: On examination in the neurosurgical clinic, the patient had hyperaesthesia from the neck down, most prominent in the hands and groins. The patient had reduced grip strength of 3/5, finger extension and abduction of 3/5, wrist flexion and extension of 3/5, elbow flexion of 4+/5, elbow extension of 4/5 and shoulder abduction of 4+/5 on the Medical Research Council power scale. Hip flexion was 3/5, with all other muscle groups in the lower limb at 4+/5. The patient had very brisk reflexes with pathological spreading in the upper and lower limbs. There was self-limiting clonus in the ankle bilaterally. Hoffmann’s and Babinski reflexes were positive bilaterally. There was a severe loss of coordination and balance. Gait was impaired; the patient required a frame to mobilise.

report.source_text: The patient underwent MRI imaging and was found to have multilevel degenerative changes of the cervical spine. At C3/4 there was a broad-based disc osteophyte protrusion causing compression of the spinal cord with T2 hyperintense signal changes within the cord. At C5/6, there was a broad-based disc osteophyte protrusion with mild narrowing of the C6 neural foramina (figure 1).

clinician.final_diagnosis: severe cervical myelopathy requiring expedited surgical decompression
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 62-year-old woman presented with progressive dysaesthetic sensory symptoms including abnormal sensations on her face, trunk, arms, and legs, along with neurological deficits such as facial dysaesthesia, back pain, multiple falls, leg weakness, poor coordination, urinary and fecal incontinence, and impaired gait. Neurological examination revealed hyperaesthesia from the neck down, muscle weakness predominantly in upper limbs and hip flexors, brisk reflexes with pathological spreading, bilateral ankle clonus, positive Hoffmann’s and Babinski reflexes, severe loss of coordination and balance, and gait impairment requiring frame use (E003). Cervical spine MRI demonstrated multilevel degenerative changes with broad-based disc osteophyte protrusions at C3/4 and C5/6, causing spinal cord compression and T2 hyperintense signal changes within the cord compatible with myelopathy (E004). This clinical and imaging evidence confirms the diagnosis of severe cervical myelopathy. Documentation of the surgical decompression procedure and subsequent clinical course were not available from the sources.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Neurological examination shows hyperaesthesia from neck down, limb weakness, pathological reflexes including ankle clonus, Hoffmann’s and Babinski signs, severe coordination loss, and impaired gait necessitating frame use.
Cervical spine MRI reveals multilevel degenerative changes with disc osteophyte protrusions causing spinal cord compression and T2 hyperintense signal within the cord at C3/4, indicating myelopathy.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Neurological examination and MRI findings localize pathology to cervical spinal cord with structural cord compression, inconsistent with isolated peripheral neuropathy.
Objective neurological signs including pathological reflexes and coordination deficits with MRI evidence of cord compression support organic myelopathy rather than purely psychogenic symptoms.
